scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The 1878 imported footprint covers St. Thomas, St. John and St. Croix. The map record uses the modern name before the 1917 transfer; periods explicitly identify Danish rule in 1878. No historical founding date is inferred from coverage.

The separate virgin-islands-danemark record in the 1715 snapshot covers Puerto Rico. It is not associated with this card. See identity-correction.json for the bounded label correction and supporting geometry comparison.

The Indigenous phase describes studied deposits from Trunk Bay and Cinnamon Bay, not a uniform ethnic identity, first settlement or population disappearance. The late Monserrate 1100 to 1200 interval is Wild’s probable stratigraphic interpretation; the broader calibrated interval is 1020 to 1200.

Hardy’s Christiansted article includes overly broad wording about all labour being performed by enslaved Africans. The card uses specific archaeological and building evidence without adopting that universal claim.

The education article has an internal discrepancy: its opening dates Annaberg’s opening to 1853, while the quoted 1856 report describes opening that year. The card states the dated report and the disagreement, without choosing an unsupported single opening date.

Hospital history is drawn from the National Register nomination, which cites Navy annual reports and Historic American Buildings Survey work. Its celebratory interpretation of colonial health reform is not adopted. No causal mortality claim, therapeutic advice or universal access to sanitation is asserted.

Music facts come from an institutional biography drawing on the named artist’s recollections, not a claim about every Virgin Islands family. No invented instruments, song lyrics or medical efficacy claims are included.

The Fireburn source names four women including Susanna Abrahamson; the card lists three examples and does not deny the fourth. It omits the false death rumour rather than repeating it as fact. Brutality is not used as a punchline.

The Danish archive dates the colony broadly to 1672 to 1917; the first period explicitly distinguishes expansion across islands. British occupations are represented separately. Period boundaries describe institutions, not verified sovereignty for every coordinate.

The citizenship and territorial account is an overview of institutional milestones, not legal advice or a claim that citizenship was granted to every resident regardless of statutory conditions. Present status was checked on the Interior Department page.
Sources and prose have been checked by the author. Independent historical review remains outstanding.
